blocks.text: Part-of-speech tagging assigns each word in a sentence its grammatical role, noun, verb, adjective, and similar categories, another specific token classification task, covered generally in an earlier topic, distinct from named entity recognition in what it actually identifies about each token.

This topic covers the common part-of-speech tag set, the challenge of words that change part of speech depending on context, and how part-of-speech tagging supports downstream language understanding tasks.
1. What Part-of-Speech Tagging Does

blocks.alt: A raw sentence goes through a POS tagger, producing tagged words

blocks.text: Part-of-speech tagging applies the token classification approach, covered in an earlier topic, to a specific goal, labeling each word with its grammatical category, this grammatical information underlies many other language understanding tasks, even when it is not the final desired output itself.
2. Common Part-of-Speech Categories

blocks.alt: NOUN, VERB, ADJ, ADV, and ADP are common part of speech categories

blocks.text: Standard part-of-speech tag sets include categories like NOUN, VERB, ADJ for adjective, ADV for adverb, and ADP for adposition, prepositions and postpositions, among others, a more granular categorization than most classification tasks covered elsewhere in this module, since natural language grammar itself has many distinct roles.

blocks.text: 3. Part-of-Speech Tagging in Practice

blocks.alt: Dog is tagged NOUN, runs is tagged VERB, and fast is tagged ADV

blocks.text: Applied to "the dog runs fast," a part-of-speech tagger identifies dog as a noun, runs as a verb, and fast as an adverb, using the same BIO-adjacent token classification structure covered in the earlier Token Tasks topic, though part-of-speech tags are typically single-token labels rather than multi-token spans.
4. Words That Change Part of Speech by Context

blocks.alt: The word book is a noun in one context and a verb in another

blocks.text: Many English words serve different grammatical roles depending on context, "book" is a noun in "read a book" but a verb in "book a flight," resolving this correctly requires the model to use surrounding sentence context rather than relying on the word alone, similar in spirit to the ambiguous entity mention challenge covered in the previous NER topic.

blocks.title: Context sensitivity is the core difficulty in POS tagging
blocks.content: A tagger that memorizes a fixed word-to-tag mapping will fail on exactly these context-dependent cases, training data needs enough examples of the same word used in different grammatical roles to teach genuine context sensitivity.

blocks.text: 5. Part-of-Speech Tags Supporting Further Analysis

blocks.alt: POS tags feed syntactic parsing, producing grammar structure

blocks.text: Part-of-speech tags commonly serve as an input to further linguistic analysis, syntactic parsing that builds a full grammatical structure of a sentence, or grammar checking tools, part-of-speech tagging itself is often a supporting step rather than a standalone end product.
6. Part-of-Speech Tagging vs Named Entity Recognition

blocks.alt: NER identifies named entities while POS identifies grammatical role

blocks.text: Both part-of-speech tagging and named entity recognition, covered in the previous topic, are token classification tasks and share the same underlying training approach, but they answer entirely different questions, grammatical role versus real-world entity identity, a word can simultaneously have a part-of-speech tag and, if it names a real entity, also have an entity tag.
7. Language-Specific Tag Sets

blocks.alt: An English tag set is compared against another language tag set

blocks.text: Part-of-speech categories are not universal across languages, some languages have grammatical distinctions English does not mark explicitly, and vice versa, a tagger fine-tuned for one language tag set generally does not transfer directly to another language without retraining on that language own tag set and data.
8. Evaluating Part-of-Speech Taggers

Since part-of-speech tags are typically single-token labels rather than multi-token spans, token-level accuracy is a more directly meaningful metric here than it was for the span-based entity-level evaluation covered in the previous NER topic, though checking accuracy specifically on known context-dependent words remains a useful additional diagnostic.
9. Common Production Use Cases

Part-of-speech tagging commonly supports grammar and writing assistance tools, information extraction pipelines that use grammatical structure to find relationships between words, and linguistic research tooling, cases where understanding sentence grammar programmatically enables further processing.
Worked Example

A team building a writing assistant tool fine-tunes a part-of-speech tagger to support grammar checking features, initial evaluation shows strong overall token-level accuracy but a closer look at errors reveals most mistakes cluster around a known set of context-dependent words like book, run, and light.

Reviewing their training data, the team finds these words were underrepresented in their less common grammatical role, adding more examples of each word used in its less frequent role measurably improves accuracy specifically on this known hard category, without needing to expand the tag set or overall dataset size much.
Common Mistakes

items: Underrepresenting context-dependent words in their less common grammatical role within training data
Assuming a tag set or trained model transfers directly to a different language without any retraining
Treating part-of-speech tagging as a standalone end goal when it is usually a supporting step for further analysis
Confusing part-of-speech tagging with named entity recognition, when the two answer fundamentally different questions

blocks.text: Practice

Write two short sentences using the same word, like book or light, in two different grammatical roles, then manually tag each word with its correct part of speech and explain what context clue makes the correct tag identifiable in each case.
Key Takeaway

Part-of-speech tagging labels each word with its grammatical role using the token classification approach covered in an earlier topic, with context-dependent words like book or run posing the main challenge since the same word can take different tags depending on surrounding sentence context, and it commonly serves as a supporting step for further linguistic analysis rather than a standalone end product.
